reading.title: The Garden Called Sukoon
paras: Ravi grew up in Sundarpur, a small town surrounded by fields and dusty roads. Life there moved slowly. Farmers walked to their fields at dawn, and in the afternoon the main bazaar grew quiet and sleepy. Most families knew one another, and children played in the lanes until the light faded.

Near Ravi’s house, however, there was an empty plot of land that nobody looked after. People often dumped broken furniture and plastic bags there. The place smelled unpleasant, and flies buzzed around it all day. Every time Ravi walked past it, he felt that such a large open space was being wasted.

One Sunday morning, Ravi suggested to his friends that they should clean the plot and turn it into a garden. At first, the idea seemed impossible because the children had no tools and very little money. Some neighbours even laughed at them, saying that a group of schoolchildren could never change a dumping ground.

Instead of giving up, the group decided to ask for help. They borrowed brooms and spades from their neighbours and collected seeds from their own homes. Every Sunday, they met to pull out weeds, level the soil, and plant saplings. They carried water in buckets from a nearby tap and covered the young plants with leaves to protect them from the heat.

Slowly, the barren plot began to change. Green shoots appeared, flowers bloomed, and the air felt fresher. Birds returned to the branches, and butterflies hovered over the beds. Villagers who once ignored the place started visiting it in the evenings to sit and relax.

The children learned that cooperation and patience could transform even a neglected corner into something beautiful. Because it brought peace to everyone, the villagers fondly called the garden Sukoon. Today the garden is looked after by a new group of young volunteers, and the plot that once embarrassed the town has become its favourite meeting place.

reading.title: The School That Opens After Sunset
paras: In Bhindol, a village of about four hundred families, the government school closes at two in the afternoon. For most children the rest of the day was spent helping at home or wandering near the highway. Two years ago, Lalita Devi, a retired teacher of sixty-eight, decided that the empty building should not stay idle. She gathered five other women from the village, none of them younger than fifty, and started an evening class from five to seven.

The class is not like a normal school. There are no bells, no uniforms and no marks. Children come when their chores are done, and the women teach whatever the children ask for — a difficult sum, a letter to a distant father, the spelling of a word heard on the radio. The older women often say that they learn as much as they teach, because a child’s question rarely has an easy answer.

Everything is made from what the village already has. Old newspapers serve as notebooks, the walls are painted with charcoal and chalk, and the class library is a tin trunk holding forty-three books donated by families. When the electricity fails, which happens often, the class moves to the veranda and continues under the light of two lanterns.

Not everyone approved at first. Some parents thought the evening class was a waste of time, and a few said girls should not go out after dark. Lalita Devi answered by walking to each house, and by the second year twenty-two girls were attending regularly. Now the panchayat has given the group a small grant for lanterns and mats, and a younger teacher comes twice a week.

Attendance is still uneven — during harvest, the class empties. Nobody minds very much. The women say that learning can wait for a day, but a family cannot, and that a class which understands this is likely to last longer than one which does not.

reading.title: Why a City Needs Old Trees
paras: A tree planted today will not shade a street properly for thirty years. That single fact explains why the oldest trees in a city are worth more than their timber, and why cutting one down is rarely a small decision. An old tree has a canopy wide enough to cool a whole lane, roots that hold soil in place during heavy rain, and hollows and cracks that insects, owls and squirrels have used for generations.

The cooling is measurable. Shade and evaporation from leaves can lower the temperature beneath a large tree by several degrees, which matters more each summer. Streets without trees stay hotter long after sunset, because concrete and tar store heat during the day and release it slowly at night. A row of trees along a road therefore does two jobs at once: it cools the air and it makes walking pleasant enough that people leave their cars at home.

Old trees also protect the ground. When rain falls hard on bare soil, it runs off quickly, carrying mud into drains and causing local flooding. Roots break the force of the rain and hold the soil together, so water soaks in slowly instead of rushing away.

None of this is visible in a photograph of a new park, which is why old trees are so easily lost. A road-widening plan may show a neat green strip of saplings and call it compensation. But a sapling cannot replace a tree that took four decades to grow; it can only, in time, become one.

Some cities have begun to count trees as public property rather than decoration. They number each old tree, record its age and health, and require permission before it is removed. In one such city, a plan to cut seventeen trees for a bus terminal was dropped after residents showed that nine of them were older than the neighbourhood itself. The terminal was built elsewhere, and no tree was cut.

reading.title: The Boy Who Kept a Rain Diary
paras: Every evening during the monsoon, a fourteen-year-old named Imran climbs to the flat roof of his house in a village near Kota and reads the rain gauge his uncle fixed there. He writes three things in a notebook: the date, the depth of water in the gauge, and one line about the sky. The notebook is cheap, the gauge is a plastic tube, and the whole habit takes four minutes.

Imran began because his father, a farmer, could never decide when to sow. The first heavy shower is not the same as the start of the rains; if seeds go into dry soil after a single shower, they may never sprout. Old farmers in the village read the sky by signs — the direction of the wind, the calling of a particular bird, the way ants move — but nobody had ever written these signs down.

After two monsoons, Imran had a page for every day. Reading it again, he noticed something the older men had felt but never stated: in his village the first steady rain of the season usually arrived about eleven days after the first heavy shower, and the gap was almost never shorter than a week. He took the notebook to the village meeting and read out the numbers. Some farmers were amused. Three tried it the following year, waited, and sowed later. Their fields came up more evenly than their neighbours’.

Word travelled slowly, which is how it usually travels in villages. A teacher at the school asked Imran to keep the diary for the whole block, and now six students share the work, taking turns with two gauges and a chart pinned in the classroom. The chart is not a forecast and Imran says so plainly. It is a record, and a record is what a forecast needs before it can be trusted.

reading.title: The Shop of Imperfect Things
paras: The shop near the bus stand in Panvel sells vegetables that no other shop will take: tomatoes with a split skin, cucumbers bent like question marks, carrots too short for a machine to peel. None of them is rotten. Each was rejected for its shape, and each would otherwise have been thrown away.

Meera, who runs the shop, learned the trade by accident. She once helped at a wedding where four crates of beans were left over because they were the wrong length for the caterer’s machines. She filled two bags and took them home, and then spent the evening wondering how much good food leaves a market every day simply because it looks unusual.

Her shop works on a simple rule: the price is half the market rate, and the customer is told why the vegetable is there. A hand-written board above the counter says, “These are the ones that were refused. They taste the same.” Some customers laugh at first. Then they come back, because a family that saves forty rupees on vegetables every week notices the saving.

The farmers gain as well. A farmer paid for a full crate no longer loses money on the part of it that the wholesale buyer refuses, and Meera collects directly from six farms, so nothing makes a second journey. Last year the shop sold about nine hundred kilograms of vegetables that would have gone to waste, and the compost heap behind the counter took what even she could not sell.

There has been one complaint, from a neighbour who says the shop makes the street untidy on collection days. Meera agrees that it does and has moved her crates inside. She is not interested in arguing that her shop is a good deed. She would rather it were simply a shop that made sense.

reading.title: Save Every Drop
paras: Water is essential for life, yet fresh water is limited and must be used wisely. Only a tiny share of the water on earth is fit for drinking, and the same supply has to serve farms, factories, hospitals and homes. In many towns, people waste water without realising it, because it arrives so easily from a tap.

A single dripping tap can waste nearly 20 litres of water in a day. That is enough drinking water for a small family. Leaking pipes in bathrooms and gardens often go unnoticed for weeks, quietly draining away a resource that millions of people walk kilometres to collect.

Simple habits can make a big difference. Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth, fixing leaking pipes, and using a bucket instead of a hose to wash vehicles can save hundreds of litres every month. Taking shorter showers and watering plants in the evening also help, because less water evaporates in the cooler air.

Schools and communities can also help by practising rainwater harvesting, a method of collecting and storing rainwater from rooftops for later use. The collected water can be used for gardening and cleaning, which reduces the pressure on the town supply. In 2024, Sunrise Public School began a “Save Every Drop” campaign. Students checked taps for leaks, placed posters around the campus, and recorded how much water different actions saved in one month.

The results showed that small efforts, when done regularly, can stop water from being wasted and protect this precious resource for the future. The school now repeats the campaign every year, and several neighbouring schools have asked the students to explain their method.

reading.title: The Reading Challenge
paras: Every October the library at Vidya Niketan runs a reading challenge. The rules are simple: a student who finishes a book writes two lines about it, and the librarian gives a sticker for the class chart. There are no prizes for the fastest reader, because the librarian has always insisted that reading quickly is not the same as reading well.

This year the challenge began with a problem. The library owned 900 books, but fewer than 200 were borrowed in a month. Most students chose the same three popular titles, and the shelves of poetry, biography and travel writing stayed untouched. The librarian added a rule: a sticker counted only if the student had not read that author before.

The result was unexpected. Class VI, which usually borrowed very little, went looking for new authors and finished 84 books. Class VII read 96, mostly mystery and animal stories. Class VIII, busy with a science project, managed only 72. Class IX, whose teacher read aloud for ten minutes at the end of every lesson, reached 108.

The chart on the library wall, however, showed something more useful than totals. The students who read the most were not the ones who read fastest; they were the ones who talked about their books. A short conversation at the issue desk, it turned out, did more for reading than any poster.

In November the librarian extended the challenge for another month, and the principal agreed to buy twenty new titles in the subjects that had been ignored. The library still owns 900 books. What changed is that more of them are being opened.

reading.title: The Waste Audit
paras: For one week in August, students at Greenfield School did something unusual: instead of emptying the bins, they opened them. Every lunchtime a team of eight weighed the waste from the canteen and the classrooms, sorted it into four materials, and wrote the figures on a chart in the corridor.

The first day was the shock. The bin outside the canteen was heavy with food — whole rotis, unopened packets of biscuits, half-eaten fruit — that had been bought and never finished. The students had expected plastic to be the biggest problem, because that is what most campaigns talk about. Paper came second, mostly worksheets printed on one side. Plastic was third, and glass, which hardly anyone thought about, was the smallest pile.

By Friday the team had 60 kilograms of waste in total. Nobody could say the school was dirty; the bins had simply hidden the truth. The team then asked a different question: what could have been avoided? Almost all the food could have been, if portions had been smaller and packets left unopened. Most of the paper could have been, if both sides had been used. The plastic and the glass could at least have been separated and sold.

The findings were read out at assembly. The canteen now serves smaller portions and keeps a “share table” where unopened packets are left for anyone who wants them. Food waste goes to a compost pit behind the kitchen, the office prints on both sides, and two bins — one for paper and glass, one for everything else — stand at the gate.
The audit cost nothing but a week of lunchtimes. The team’s report ended with a line that the principal has printed on a card above every bin: “We cannot manage what we have never weighed.”

questions.q: How much food waste was collected in the week?
questions.why: According to the table, food waste came to 25 kilograms.

questions.q: Which material made up the largest share of the waste?
questions.why: Food was 25 kilograms, more than paper (18), plastic (12) or glass (5).

questions.q: What was the total amount of waste collected in one week?
questions.why: The total is 25 + 18 + 12 + 5 = 60 kilograms.

questions.q: How much more food waste than plastic waste was collected?
questions.why: Food was 25 kilograms and plastic 12, so the difference is 25 − 12 = 13 kilograms.

questions.q: If the food, paper and glass were all kept out of the landfill, how much waste would still go to it?
questions.why: Food, paper and glass together weigh 25 + 18 + 5 = 48 kilograms, so the 12 kilograms of plastic would still go to the landfill.

questions.q: How many days did the audit last? (one word)
questions.why: The audit ran for one week, from the first day to Friday — five days.

questions.q: Find words from the passage which mean the following: (one word each)

parts.label: (a) decayed food waste used to enrich soil —
(b) the amount of food served to one person —

questions.why: Food waste goes to a ‘compost’ pit, and a ‘portion’ is the amount of food served to one person.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: “Plastic made up the largest share of the waste.”
questions.why: Food was the largest at 25 kilograms; plastic was third at 12 kilograms.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: The students were surprised because ____________.
opts: they had expected plastic to be the biggest problem
the canteen had closed for the week
glass weighed the most of all
questions.why: The students had expected plastic to be the biggest problem, because that is what most campaigns talk about.

questions.why: Instead of emptying the bins, the team weighed the waste and sorted it into four materials.

reading.title: Cycle to School Week
paras: For five days in November, students at Nirmala School were asked to leave the car at home and come by bicycle. The idea came from the science club, which had counted the traffic outside the gate: between 7.40 and 8.00 in the morning, forty-one cars waited at the same crossing, and most carried a single child.

The first morning was chaos. Bicycles arrived from every direction, the racks were too few, and a boy who had not ridden for two years fell at the gate. By Tuesday two teachers were guiding the younger riders in from the corner, and the head boy had drawn a route map on the notice board. On Wednesday a puncture repair kit appeared, donated by a cycle shop down the road.

By Friday the racks were full long before the bell. The club counted the cyclists every morning and wrote the numbers on a chart. Monday’s figure, 120, looked unremarkable. Tuesday’s was 138. Wednesday’s 150 was helped by a clear sky. Thursday dipped to 132 when a shower fell at seven. Friday reached 160, the highest of the week, when the club promised a cricket match for the class with the most riders.

The club then did the arithmetic that made the week worth repeating. Each cyclist lived about three kilometres from school, so the week’s rides covered 2,100 kilometres that would otherwise have been driven. At 120 grams of carbon dioxide per kilometre, that is roughly 252 kilograms of the gas that never entered the air above the school gate.

Not everything worked. Two students live eleven kilometres away and came by bus instead, and one class had no cycle at all. The club has asked the panchayat for a covered rack and a spare set of cycles, so that next year the week is not limited to those who already own a bicycle.

questions.q: On which day did the most students cycle to school?
questions.why: Friday reached 160 cyclists, the highest figure in the table.

questions.q: How many students cycled during the whole week?
questions.why: The total is 120 + 138 + 150 + 132 + 160 = 700 student-trips.

questions.q: What was the average number of cyclists per day?
questions.why: The week’s total is 700 over five days, so the average is 700 ÷ 5 = 140.

questions.q: How many more students cycled on Friday than on Monday?
questions.why: Friday had 160 cyclists and Monday 120, so the difference is 160 − 120 = 40.

questions.q: If every cyclist rode 3 kilometres each day, how far did the week’s rides cover altogether?
questions.why: 700 rides of 3 kilometres each cover 700 × 3 = 2,100 kilometres.

questions.q: How many days did the cycle week last? (one word)
questions.why: The passage says that for five days students were asked to come by bicycle.

questions.q: Find words from the passage which mean the following: (one word each)

parts.label: (a) a person who rides a bicycle —
(b) a small hole in a tyre —

questions.why: A ‘cyclist’ rides a bicycle, and a ‘puncture’ is a small hole in a tyre.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: “More students cycled on Thursday than on Wednesday.”
questions.why: Thursday had 132 cyclists and Wednesday 150, so fewer cycled on Thursday.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: Thursday’s figure was lower because ____________.
questions.why: The passage says Thursday dipped to 132 when a shower fell at seven.

questions.q: How many kilograms of carbon dioxide were kept out of the air? (one word)
questions.why: At 120 grams per kilometre over 2,100 kilometres, roughly 252 kilograms of carbon dioxide were not released.

reading.title: Sleep, Screens and School
paras: Last term the school nurse asked 300 students one question that turned out to be harder to answer than expected: how much do you sleep? The answers were collected without names, so nobody had to pretend.

Students were then grouped by a second question — how long they looked at a screen after nine at night, whether a phone, a television or a laptop. The pattern in the answers was clear. The 90 students who kept screens out of the last hour before bed reported 8.5 hours of sleep on an average school night. The 120 who used a screen for up to an hour reported 8.0. The 60 who used one for one to two hours reported 7.2, and the 30 who used one for more than two hours reported only 6.4.

The nurse was careful about what the numbers mean. A survey of this kind cannot prove that screens cause short sleep; it may be that students who sleep badly are the ones who reach for a screen. What it can do is point at a habit worth testing. She asked one class to try a two-week experiment: phones charged outside the bedroom, no screens after nine. The class’s reported sleep rose by about forty minutes, and, more surprisingly, the number of students arriving late fell.

Not every family could follow the advice. In several homes the only screen is shared, and a study hour after dinner is the only quiet time a student has. The nurse’s final report says so plainly, and suggests a smaller rule that almost any household can keep: the last twenty minutes before sleep should belong to something that is not a screen.

questions.q: Which group reported the most sleep?
opts: Students with no screen after 9 pm
Students with up to 1 hour of screen time
Students with 1–2 hours of screen time
Students with more than 2 hours of screen time
questions.why: The group with no screen after 9 pm reported 8.5 hours, the highest in the table.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep did the group with more than two hours of screen time report?
questions.why: According to the table, the group with more than two hours of screen time reported only 6.4 hours.

questions.q: How many students took part in the survey?
questions.why: The four groups are 90 + 120 + 60 + 30 = 300 students.

questions.q: How many hours less sleep did the 1–2 hour group get than the no-screen group?
questions.why: 8.5 − 7.2 = 1.3 hours less sleep for the 1–2 hour group.

questions.q: How many students used a screen for more than two hours after 9 pm?
questions.why: According to the table, 30 students used a screen for more than two hours.

questions.q: After what time at night was screen time counted? (one word)
questions.why: Students were grouped by how long they looked at a screen after nine at night.

questions.q: Find words from the passage which mean the following: (one word each)

parts.label: (b) a set of questions used to collect information —

questions.why: The answers were collected ‘anonymously’, and a ‘survey’ is a set of questions used to collect information.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: “The survey proves that screens cause short sleep.”
questions.why: The nurse says a survey of this kind cannot prove that screens cause short sleep.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: In the two-week experiment, the class’s reported sleep rose by ____________.
questions.why: The passage says the class’s reported sleep rose by about forty minutes.

questions.q: Where were phones charged during the experiment? (one word)
questions.why: The experiment asked for phones to be charged outside the bedroom.

litExtracts.label: Extract 1
litExtracts.title: Paper Boats — Rabindranath Tagore
text: I launch my paper boats and look up into the sky and see the little clouds setting the white bulging sails.
I know not what playmate of mine in the sky sends them down the air to race with my boats!
When night comes I bury my face in my arms and dream that my paper boats float on and on under the midnight stars.
The fairies of sleep are sailing in them, and the lading is their baskets full of dreams.

questions.q: What does the child see in the sky when he looks up?
options: Little clouds that look like white sails
The moon rising above the stream
questions.why: “I look up into the sky and see the little clouds setting the white bulging sails” — the clouds are imagined as sails.

questions.q: What does “playmate of mine in the sky” suggest?
options: He has a friend who lives in another land
He imagines the clouds as companions who send boats to race with his
Other children are flying kites with him
Someone in the sky writes letters to him
questions.why: The child treats the clouds as playmates racing his boats — a child’s way of turning the sky into a playground.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: Paper boats raced by cloud playmates and sailed by the fairies of sleep: “Paper Boats” by Rabindranath Tagore.

questions.q: The last two lines show that the child’s boats carry
options: his name and the name of his village
dreams, sailed by the fairies of sleep
letters for his friends across the stream
questions.why: “The fairies of sleep are sailing in them, and the lading is their baskets full of dreams.”

questions.q: Which word in the extract means the goods carried in a boat?
questions.why: “Lading” is the cargo a boat carries — here, baskets full of dreams.

litExtracts.label: Extract 2
litExtracts.title: A Funny Man — Natalie Joan
text: One day a funny kind of man
Came walking down this street
He wore a shoe upon his head
And hats upon his feet.
He raised the shoe and smiled at me,
His manners were polite;
But never had I seen before
Such a funny sounding sight.

questions.q: What did the man wear on his head?
questions.why: “He wore a shoe upon his head / And hats upon his feet” — everything about him is the wrong way round.

questions.q: “His manners were polite” means that the man
options: spoke in a very loud voice
behaved in a courteous, well-mannered way
questions.why: Polite manners are courteous behaviour — his behaviour is courteous even though his appearance is absurd.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The man with a shoe on his head and hats on his feet: “A Funny Man” by Natalie Joan.

questions.q: “Such a funny sounding sight” is an example of
questions.why: A sight cannot really be “sounding”; the poet mixes seeing and hearing to show how strange the man looked.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means strange and amusing?
questions.why: “Funny” is repeated through the poem for exactly this meaning — odd and laughable.

litExtracts.label: Extract 3
litExtracts.title: A Funny Man — Natalie Joan
text: He said, 'Allow me to present
Your Highness with a rose.'
And taking out a currant bun
He held it to my nose.
I staggered back against the wall
And then I answered, 'Well!
I never saw a rose with such
A funny looking smell.'

questions.q: What did the man actually hold out as a “rose”?
questions.why: “And taking out a currant bun / He held it to my nose.” The “rose” is only a bun.

questions.q: Why did he hold it to the poet’s nose?
options: So that she could smell it, as one smells a rose
So that she would take it from him
Because it was too hot to hold
To hide his face from her
questions.why: A rose is offered to be smelt; he follows the ritual of offering a flower, but with a bun.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: “Your Highness”, the currant bun offered as a rose: “A Funny Man” by Natalie Joan.

questions.q: Why did the poet stagger back against the wall?
options: She was pushed by the man
She was startled by the absurd trick played on her
She wanted to run away from the street
questions.why: “I staggered back” — she is taken aback by being offered a bun as if it were a rose.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means moved unsteadily?
questions.why: To stagger is to move or step unsteadily, as she does against the wall.

litExtracts.label: Extract 4
litExtracts.title: A Funny Man — Natalie Joan
text: He then began to sing a song,
And sat down on the ground;
You never heard in all your life
Such a funny feeling sound.
'My friend, why do you wear two hats
Upon your feet?' I said.
He turned the other way about,
And hopped home on his head.

questions.q: What question did the poet ask the man?
options: Why he wore a shoe on his head
Why he wore two hats upon his feet
Where he lived in the town
Why he was singing on the ground
questions.why: “My friend, why do you wear two hats / Upon your feet?” I said.

questions.q: “Such a funny feeling sound” suggests that the sound
options: was too soft to be heard
seemed to be felt as well as heard
questions.why: The poet mixes hearing with feeling, just as she mixed sight with sound earlier.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The man who sang on the ground and “hopped home on his head”: “A Funny Man” by Natalie Joan.

questions.q: What does the last line tell us about the man?
options: He was angry at the question
He answered with another absurd action instead of words
He could not understand the question
He was in a hurry to reach home before dark
questions.why: Asked a sensible question, he simply turns about and hops home on his head — the nonsense never stops.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means jumped on one foot?
questions.why: “Hopped home on his head” — to hop is to spring along on one foot.

litExtracts.label: Extract 5
litExtracts.title: Travel — Edna St. Vincent Millay
text: The railroad track is miles away,
And the day is loud with voices speaking,
Yet there isn't a train goes by all day
But I hear its whistle shrieking.
All night there isn't a train goes by,
Though the night is still for sleep and dreaming,
But I see its cinders red on the sky,
And hear its engine steaming.

questions.q: How far away is the railroad track?
options: On the other side of the hill
questions.why: The poem opens with “The railroad track is miles away” — yet she notices every train.

questions.q: “The day is loud with voices speaking” means that the day is
options: full of the noise of people talking
full of music from the train
questions.why: The day is noisy with human chatter, and still she catches the whistle above it.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The railroad miles away and the whistle she cannot stop hearing: “Travel” by Edna St. Vincent Millay.

questions.q: Even though the track is far away, the speaker says that
options: she never actually hears a train
she hears the whistle of every train that passes
she walks to the track every evening
the trains stop running at night
questions.why: “Yet there isn’t a train goes by all day / But I hear its whistle shrieking” — she hears them all.

questions.q: Which word in the extract describes a sharp, shrill cry?
questions.why: “Whistle shrieking” — shrieking is a sharp, piercing sound, and it makes the whistle seem alive.

litExtracts.label: Extract 6
litExtracts.title: Travel — Edna St. Vincent Millay
text: All night there isn't a train goes by,
Though the night is still for sleep and dreaming,
But I see its cinders red on the sky,
And hear its engine steaming.
My heart is warm with the friends I make,
And better friends I'll not be knowing,
Yet there isn't a train I wouldn't take,
No matter where it's going.

questions.q: When does the speaker see the red cinders on the sky?
questions.why: “All night there isn’t a train goes by … But I see its cinders red on the sky.”

questions.q: “The night is still for sleep and dreaming” tells us that the night is
options: full of the noise of trains
questions.why: The night is silent and made for rest — yet she is still watching and listening for trains.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: Cinders at night and “no matter where it’s going”: “Travel” by Edna St. Vincent Millay.

questions.q: What do these lines show about the speaker?
options: She dislikes the place she lives in
The thought of the train is always on her mind
She is afraid of travelling alone
questions.why: She notices the train by day and by night, even while valuing her friends — travel fills her thoughts.

questions.q: Which word in the extract suggests the engine is giving off steam?
questions.why: “Hear its engine steaming” — steaming shows the engine letting out steam as it runs.

litExtracts.label: Extract 7
litExtracts.title: My Dear Soldiers — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
text: Climbing the heights or striding the valleys
Defending the deserts or guarding the marshes
Surveillance in seas and by securing the air
Prime of your youth given to the nation!!

questions.q: Which places does the poet say the soldiers guard?
options: Only the mountains and the deserts
Heights, valleys, deserts, marshes, seas and the air
questions.why: The lines list heights, valleys, deserts, marshes, seas and air — the soldiers guard every kind of terrain.

questions.q: “Surveillance in seas and by securing the air” means that the soldiers
options: travel by ship and by plane
watch over the sea and guard the air space
questions.why: Surveillance is close watching — they keep watch at sea and secure the country’s air.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: Heights, valleys, deserts and “Prime of your youth given to the nation!!”: “My Dear Soldiers” by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

questions.q: “Prime of your youth given to the nation” shows the soldiers’
questions.why: “Prime of youth” is the strongest, best time of life — they spend it in service of the country.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means the best or most vigorous period?
questions.why: Prime means the peak — the best years of a person’s life.

litExtracts.label: Extract 8
litExtracts.title: My Dear Soldiers — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
text: Wind chimes of my land vibrate your feat
We pray for you brave men!!
May the Lord bless you all!!

questions.q: What do the “wind chimes of my land” do?
options: Sound in honour of the soldiers’ achievement
Ring to wake the soldiers each morning
questions.why: “Wind chimes of my land vibrate your feat” — the land itself seems to ring out for their deed.

questions.q: “Vibrate your feat” means that the chimes
options: make a sound in praise of the soldiers’ achievement
shake because of the strong wind
are played by the soldiers themselves
questions.why: Their feat — their brave achievement — is what the chimes of the land answer with sound.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The wind chimes, the prayer for “brave men” and the blessing: “My Dear Soldiers” by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

questions.q: The poem ends with a prayer, which shows the poet’s
options: gratitude and goodwill towards the soldiers
questions.why: “We pray for you brave men!! / May the Lord bless you all!!” — the prayer is thanks and a wish for their safety.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a remarkable achievement?
questions.why: A feat is a brave or remarkable act — here, the soldiers’ service to the nation.

litExtracts.label: Extract 1
text: A big bright tear splashed down her nose. And another. A kingfisher swept down, its wings an arrow of blue in the sunlight. And a green lizard slithered down to the river’s edge to bask in the sun.
“Dear, dear!” said a sleepy, murmuring voice, “What’s the matter?”

Jahnavi was startled, because she was sure she had been quite alone. It couldn’t have been the lizard. And the kingfisher was up in the thicket of bamboo eating the fish it had caught. It couldn’t be the parrots, because parrots shrieked and this was such a sleepy voice. She looked around her. There wasn’t a soul in sight. She was rather scared and wanted to run away.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: Jahnavi believed she was alone by the river before she heard the voice.
questions.why: “Jahnavi was startled, because she was sure she had been quite alone.” The voice took her by surprise.

questions.q: What swept down over the river, described as “an arrow of blue”?
questions.why: “A kingfisher swept down, its wings an arrow of blue in the sunlight” — the blue wings are the arrow.

questions.q: Why did Jahnavi decide that the parrots could not be the ones speaking?
options: Parrots shrieked, and this voice was sleepy and low
The parrots were too far away to be heard
questions.why: “It couldn’t be the parrots, because parrots shrieked and this was such a sleepy voice.”

questions.q: What does “There wasn’t a soul in sight” tell us?
options: She could see nobody anywhere around her
She was the only person who lived there
She had lost her way in the bamboo
questions.why: “Not a soul in sight” means not a single person was visible — though someone was clearly speaking.

questions.q: The word “murmuring” describes a voice that is
questions.why: To murmur is to speak in a low, soft voice — which is why the voice sounded sleepy.

litExtracts.label: Extract 2
text: Jahnavi saw the teacher walking up the steps to their gate the next evening when she was lighting the lamp. She could see her father scratching his cheek the way he did when he was worried and the teacher was nodding and saying something she couldn’t make out.

And Mother said, “Little Jahnavi, I shall miss you when you go to school. Girls should learn as much as they want. When I was your age, I wanted to go to school, but your grandmother said ‘No’, but now, I am glad the teacher came to talk to your father.”
And Jahnavi said, “Mother, when I grow up, I’ll be a teacher and I’ll go from house to house in our village and ask all the little girls to come to my school.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: Jahnavi’s mother was unhappy that Jahnavi would go to school.
questions.why: Mother says she will miss her, but also that “Girls should learn as much as they want” — she is glad, not unhappy.

questions.q: Who came to the family’s gate the next evening?
questions.why: “Jahnavi saw the teacher walking up the steps to their gate the next evening.”

questions.q: What was Jahnavi’s father doing while the teacher spoke to him?
options: Scratching his cheek, as he did when worried
questions.why: “She could see her father scratching his cheek the way he did when he was worried.”

questions.q: Mother’s words show that she
options: did not want Jahnavi to study
believed girls should learn as much as they want
wanted Jahnavi to stay at home and mind Appu
questions.why: She says she wanted to go to school herself and that “Girls should learn as much as they want.”

questions.q: What does Jahnavi say she will do when she grows up?
options: Become a teacher and bring the village girls to her school
Work in the fields with her mother
Travel to the sea in Chandu’s catamaran
Write a book about the river
questions.why: She promises to be a teacher and “go from house to house … and ask all the little girls to come to my school.”

litExtracts.label: Extract 3
text: Doctor Dolittle was sitting in his kitchen talking with the Cat’s-food-Man who had come to see him with a stomach-ache.
“Why don’t you give up being a people’s doctor, and be an animal doctor?” asked the Cat’s-food-Man.
The parrot, Polynesia, was sitting in the window looking out at the rain and singing a sailor song to herself. She stopped singing and started to listen.
“You know all about animals—much more than what these vets here do. That book you wrote—about cats, why, it’s wonderful! … You might have been a cat yourself. You know the way they think.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The Cat’s-food-Man had come to Doctor Dolittle because of a stomach-ache.
questions.why: The opening line says he “had come to see him with a stomach-ache” — he was the patient.

questions.q: What did the Cat’s-food-Man advise the Doctor to do?
options: Give up being a people’s doctor and become an animal doctor
questions.why: His advice is direct: “give up being a people’s doctor, and be an animal doctor.”

questions.q: Who was Polynesia?
questions.why: “The parrot, Polynesia, was sitting in the window” — she is the Doctor’s parrot.

questions.q: What does Polynesia’s behaviour in this passage suggest about her?
options: She is asleep through the conversation
She is interested in what the visitor says about the Doctor
She is trying to leave the house
questions.why: She stops singing and listens — she follows the advice being given, then repeats it to the Doctor.

questions.q: The Cat’s-food-Man calls his wife Theodosia a “scholar”, which means
questions.why: A scholar is a learned person — he says she read the Doctor’s book to him.

litExtracts.label: Extract 4
text: “But animals don’t always speak with their mouths,” said the parrot in a high voice, raising her eyebrows. “They talk with their ears, with their feet, with their tails—with everything. Sometimes they don’t want to make a noise. Do you see now the way he’s twitching up one side of his nose?”
“What’s that mean?” asked the Doctor.
“That means, ‘Can’t you see that it has stopped raining?’” Polynesia answered. “He is asking you a question. Dogs nearly always use their noses for asking questions.”
After a while, with the parrot’s help, the Doctor got to learn the language of the animals so well that he could talk to them himself and understand everything they said.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: According to Polynesia, animals sometimes speak without making any noise.
questions.why: She says they talk “with their ears, with their feet, with their tails” and that “Sometimes they don’t want to make a noise.”

questions.q: What was the dog doing with one side of his nose?
questions.why: Polynesia asks, “Do you see now the way he’s twitching up one side of his nose?”

questions.q: What did the nose twitch actually mean?
options: “Can’t you see that it has stopped raining?”
questions.why: Polynesia translates it for the Doctor: “That means, ‘Can’t you see that it has stopped raining?’”

questions.q: What does Polynesia’s explanation show about animals?
options: They communicate with many parts of their bodies
They speak only in the morning
questions.why: Ears, feet, tails, noses — animals use their whole bodies to talk, not only their mouths.

questions.q: The word “twitching” in the passage means
questions.why: A twitch is a small, sudden movement — the dog’s nose jerks up on one side.

litExtracts.label: Extract 5
text: MRS. SHAW: I can’t tell you everything, but you’ll always be right if you’re kind to people. Say things that will please them. Then they’ll like you. Laugh a lot, and try to make them laugh too. And if everyone stops talking, say something to make them talk again. They don’t want to sit here and look at the floor without speaking.
MARY: What shall I do when they want to go?
MRS. SHAW: Ask them to stay a little while longer. Just say, “Must you go? Can’t you stay?” or something like that. You like them and you want them to stay, and you must let them understand that.
MARY: That’s not very hard, is it? I’ll remember that. “Must you go? Can’t you stay?”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: Mrs. Shaw tells Mary to look glad when the guests want to leave.
questions.why: She says the opposite: Mary must not jump up gladly, but ask them to stay a little longer.

questions.q: According to Mrs. Shaw, Mary will “always be right” if she
options: says exactly what her mother tells her
